title: ADAPT Lab at CCNY
text:
The ADAPT Lab provides opportunities for current CCNY undergraduate and graduate students to become meaningfully involved in the research we do as a research assistant (RA).
We are a great fit for students interested in research in at least one of the following topic areas: stress, coping, trauma, couples, intimate partner violence, LGBTQ+ mental health, and psychotherapy research.
Students working in the lab can expect to receive training and direct experience in the following areas depending on current ongoing projects: theories and methods in stress and relationship science, study recruitment, project administration, data collection (including longitudinal and behavioral observation methods), data management, observational coding, statistical analysis, and for motivated students, manuscript writing and publication.
To apply to be an RA in the ADAPT Lab, please reach out directly to Dr. Sullivan (tsullivan1@ccny.cuny.edu) with a brief blurb about you, why you want to work in the lab, and what types of experience you’d hope to gain. Please include a current resume or CV and “ADAPT Lab: RA Position Inquiry” in the title. You should be willing to commit to at least two semesters in the lab. RAs can serve on a volunteer basis or receive course credit for their work in the lab.
Dr. Sullivan does not currently serve as a primary mentor for PhD students in the Clinical Psychology Program at CCNY or in the Health Psychology and Clinical Science Program at The Graduate Center at CUNY. He does not review applications for these programs, but he is open to serving on dissertation committees and to mentoring thesis projects for current CCNY master’s students.
Last update: October 2026

title: ADAPT Lab at CCNY
text:
Stress can profoundly affect our lives, yet people do not experience stress equally. The Adversity and Diversity in Advancing Personalized Treatment (ADAPT) Lab at The City College of New York focuses on how and why stress impacts people differently so we can use this knowledge to make therapy better. We study how exposure to stress and people’s reactions to it shape their interpersonal relationships and mental health–particularly among people who experience especially intense (i.e., trauma) or notably chronic types of stress (e.g., LGBTQ+ stigma).
Directed by Dr. T.J. Sullivan, the ADAPT Lab at CCNY explores these topics because people place tremendous trust in their therapists to understand who they are, where they come from, and the nuances of what they’re struggling with right now. To provide effective treatment tailored to each person, therapists need to know how to best address the complex ways that early and ongoing stress influences people’s lives in subtle and not-so-subtle ways. We help advance this knowledge through basic and applied research.
Please note: This website is an active work in progress.

title: People
text:
Dr. T.J. Sullivan (he/him) is a licensed clinical psychologist and an Assistant Professor in the Mental Health Counseling Program, housed within the Department of Psychology at The City College of New York, where he directs the Adversity and Diversity in Personalized Treatment (ADAPT) Lab. His research broadly spans stress and relationship science to inform personalized therapy and principled clinical decision-making. Dr. Sullivan studies how stress impacts people differently based on the unique ways that social contexts shape stress exposures and reactions, particularly among the LGBTQ+ community. Specifically, he focuses on how interpersonal support and coping processes may protect people’s mental health and social functioning in the face of stress, as well as how different stressor characteristics such as chronic targeted rejection may increase risk for negative psychological and social outcomes. Dr. Sullivan completed his B.A. in Psychology and French and Francophone Studies (Minor in Dance) at Penn State University, his Ph.D. in Clinical Psychology at Stony Brook University, his clinical residency at VA Puget Sound Healthcare System Seattle Division, and a postdoctoral clinical research fellowship in LGBTQ+ mental health at Yale School of Public Health.

title: Overview
text:
Topics studied in the ADAPT Lab at CCNY span basic stress and relationship science to psychotherapy research. Click here to skip down to current studies in the lab.
The following core questions guide our work:


Because conclusions drawn from stress research are only as valid as the measures used, a core component of the research conducted in the ADAPT Lab optimizes ways to assess stress processes. We focus on: (a) how to best measure stress constructs psychometrically, and (b) methodological approaches to increase ecological validity in studying stress processes.
Prior work in this area includes: -MI -dating stress -behav observation



Especially intense (e.g., trauma) and notably chronic (e.g., stigma due to marginalized identities) forms of stress often, but not always, hurt people’s mental health and social relationships. However, the complex processes by which stress does and does not harm people remain elusive, so we focus on understanding pathways in and out of this risk. Specifically, we examine (a) how interpersonal support and coping processes may weaken the harms of stress (e.g., bring partners closer together), and (b) how characteristics of specific stressors may strengthen such harms (e.g., drive partners apart).
Prior work in this area includes: -multimethod -diss & ipv -honors thesis



Our lab focuses on how we can align innovations in stress and relationship science to encourage principled decision-making and case formulation in therapy, as well as how we can better understand how therapy works.
Prior work in this area includes: -ladi -qual -tx relationship
